title: Addressing Instrument-Outcome Confounding in Mendelian Randomization through Representation Learning
claim: Modeling disentangled latent sources makes valid instruments visible, whereas the marginal graph without them leaves every observed instrument invalid.
layout: 2 panels side-by-side, left DAG vs right ADMG, shaded latent nodes
description: Two causal graphs sit side by side on a white background, drawn in black and grey. The left panel is a DAG. Observed instruments Z1, Z2 and Z3 are white circles on the far left. Next to them are grey shaded latent nodes U1, U2 and U3, which have arrows into the Z nodes. Each U also points to the treatment D, and D points to the outcome Y. A grey hidden confounder H points to D, Y and U1. The right panel is an ADMG over the same variables, with no U nodes. Z1, Z2, Z3 and D are linked by curved and straight bidirected arrows, and H points to Z1, Z2, Z3, D and Y. The dense arrow web on the right contrasts with the structured latent layers on the left. The eye goes first to the grey nodes and the tangle of edges.
caption: Left: DAG with disentangled latent variables that generate $Z$, where $U_2$ and $U_3$, if observed, are valid instruments for $D$ with respect to $Y$. Right: ADMG without considering the disentangled latent variables, $Z_1$ to $Z_3$ are all invalid instruments due to $Z_1$'s violation of exchangability.\protect\footnotemark
abstract: Mendelian Randomization (MR) is a prominent observational epidemiological research method designed to address unobserved confounding when estimating causal effects. However, core assumptions -- particularly the independence between instruments and unobserved confounders -- are often violated due to population stratification or assortative mating. Leveraging the increasing availability of multi-environment data, we propose a representation learning framework that exploits cross-environment invariance to recover latent exogenous components of genetic instruments. We provide theoretical guarantees for identifying these latent instruments under various mixing mechanisms and demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through simulations and semi-synthetic experiments using data from the All of Us Research Hub.
